title: When an Estimate Becomes a Warranty: Climate Data and Revision Risk under the CISG
abstract: When a supplier revises an earlier greenhouse gas emissions estimate, the discrepancy may expose a breach of a contractual undertaking, reflect an evidentiary improvement upon a calculation that was properly performed, or capture upstream activities falling outside the scope of the original agreement. Allocating the resulting investigation and recalculation expenses raises foundational questions of contractual responsibility that mandatory climate-reporting regimes do not resolve on their own terms. Drawing upon a hypothetical cross-border sale of manufactured goods between a Singaporean seller and an Australian buyer, this doctrinal study examines how the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods governs the cost of investigating and correcting historical production data. The analysis separates the object of a contractual promise from its standard of performance, demonstrating that an undertaking to apply a prescribed calculation method may impose strict liability as to process without warranting the numerical accuracy of the resulting figure, whilst an accurate report may simultaneously reveal that the delivered goods exceed an agreed carbon ceiling. Competing scholarly accounts concerning obligations of effort and exemption from damages under article 79 are evaluated by tracing their consequences for the buyer's remaining non-damages remedies. The study further critiques the automatic extension of the goods-centric notice and cut-off periods under articles 38 and 39 to independently due reporting obligations, whilst acknowledging both the commercial rationale for the analogy and the risk of opportunistic pleading designed to revive lost conformity claims. By connecting the classification of primary obligations to post-delivery evidence and the recoverability of verification costs, the article demonstrates how targeted contractual mechanisms governing record access, timely correction, and reassessment funding can preserve effective legal recourse whilst distinguishing defective performance from subsequent improvements in emissions data.

title: Equal Standing and the Justification of Social Power
abstract: A right to care may be vindicated only after the recipient has endured an interruption and an unpaid caregiver has supplied the missing work. That interval raises a question about equal standing: how can institutional authority remain justified when the person contesting it cannot safely withdraw? Drawing on political philosophy and doctrinal analysis of English care and capacity law, this article develops a principle of continuing responsibility for the burdens of complaint and transition. Rawlsian representation is extended to include people permanently unable to exercise the moral powers assumed in his conception of the citizen. A bounded duty of material assistance is defended against Nozick’s entitlement theory, with explicit limits on compulsory personal service. The legal analysis distinguishes statutory responsibility, fiduciary loyalty and authority to decide for another, and examines the Supreme Court’s 2026 revision of the deprivation-of-liberty test. Existing complaint and advocacy duties provide a foundation, but do not settle every question of interim continuity. The proposed reforms place responsibility for replacement arrangements on the commissioning authority, preserve caregivers’ independent claims and require scrutiny of the evidence used to justify intervention. A scarcity example tests those protections against an equally urgent competing claim. The contribution is an account of how institutions should allocate the work, risk and irrecoverable losses of securing care while dependence continues.

title: Authority to Settle: Public Law and the Enforceability of Investor-State Mediated Settlements
abstract: Settlement of an investment dispute may require powers distributed among ministers, legislatures and regulators, leaving the negotiator dependent on other institutions for expenditure and the public acts promised in return for the investor’s release. This article examines how a record of completed domestic approval can acquire evidential and legal significance in foreign proceedings. It reads the Singapore Convention on Mediation alongside institutional rules, international law on official conduct and public instruments from Peru, Viet Nam and Pakistan, while using India and Thailand to establish the limits of treating negotiated outcomes as mediated agreements. The proposed authority certificate would identify the approved text, competent institutions, fiscal powers and outstanding conditions. Domestic legislation would give that record presumptive evidential force and protect reliance against narrowly defined internal irregularities, subject to constitutional review and third-party rights. An investment treaty could reinforce the protection through a specific undertaking and remedy; contractual incorporation would depend on the law applied by the enforcing forum. A certificate-based reservation offers a defensible proposed classification of government settlements, although its consequences outside the reserving State remain unresolved. The argument specifies the risks that public institutions may lawfully allocate through certification and the evidence on which that allocation depends. Approval would consequently support a more durable compromise while leaving appropriation, regulatory competence and execution immunity to the legal rules governing each.

title: Insurance Underwriting and Social Protection in ASEAN
abstract: Governments that purchase or mandate insurance determine both the risks transferred to an insurer and the losses left with the people they intend to protect. This article examines responsibility for that retained exposure through a functional comparison of insurance and social protection law in Singapore, the Philippines, Malaysia and the Lao People’s Democratic Republic. Residual loss is defined against a programme’s protective purpose and distinguished from an unpaid contractual or statutory benefit. The distinction connects underwriting disputes to public decisions about coverage and the expenditure of sovereign insurance proceeds. Malaysian disclosure remedies and Philippine restrictions on discriminatory underwriting reveal different evidential demands: reconstructing the insurer’s historical response to accurate information and establishing the grounds actually used to exclude an applicant. A constructed index-insurance model further demonstrates that equal expected payments can leave markedly different shortfalls during severe loss. These findings support a proposed duty requiring public authorities to justify foreseeable retained exposure when selecting or renewing insurance and allocating its proceeds. The duty combines preservation of the evidence supporting those choices with review by a body competent to reconsider them. Doing so renders public choices accountable after the insurer has performed, while preserving the distinct remedies through which beneficiaries enforce benefits already owed.

title: Teaching and Assessing Legal Reasoning with Generative AI in Thai Universities
abstract: An accurate legal memorandum prepared with generative artificial intelligence may conceal uncertainty about the proposition on which its advice depends. For a university awarding credit, the difficulty is to establish which legal judgements the student can defend when preparation has been assisted and questioning may itself supply part of the answer. This article combines a critical narrative review with doctrinal analysis of Thai law to develop an assessment sequence comprising a prepared memorandum, observed justification and controlled factual variation. Its central argument attaches independence to the intellectual operation being assessed. Finding a provision, interpreting a provision identified by an examiner and applying a supplied interpretation warrant different attributions of achievement. A fictional licensing problem, followed by Thai administrative provisions and a limited Singapore comparison, demonstrates how source selection, statutory language and evidence determine those attributions. Thai qualification standards and institutional policies provide the setting for examining the proposal’s fairness, workload and treatment of student records. The article also distinguishes the evidence needed to mark present understanding from that needed to investigate misconduct, retention or an improvement caused by teaching. It proposes separate studies of assessment validity and educational effectiveness before wider adoption. By relating credit to the reasoning a student actually performs, the framework gives universities a more precise basis for certifying judgement in advice on which other people may rely.
